fullText:
Recommended work from Meta on harnesses for proactive agents.

The ProPerAgent harness raises accuracy from at most 15% with standard memory baselines to 38%, without changing the model's weights.

But this success requires both a useful response and correct timing.

The harness controls how personal memories reach the model as it observes the user's surroundings.

First, the model identifies objects in view. A retrieval module uses those objects to search a graph of past experiences, preferences, and constraints.

A separate LLM call then checks whether the retrieved memories justify offering help now. It filters out distracting or already resolved information and returns one concise piece of evidence, or nothing. The model uses that evidence and the current view to decide whether to speak or stay silent.

That filtering step matters. Removing it drops accuracy from 37.3% to 24.0% in an ablation. Across the full harness, unnecessary interventions on clips that require silence fall to 15.3%, compared with 77.3% or 84.0% for standard RAG in the two evaluation modes.

The harness also reaches 37.5% with Qwen3.8-27B without training. Additional RL training on that model raises accuracy to 42.4% by penalizing premature and repeated interventions.

For proactive assistants, the harness needs to check whether a memory warrants an interruption before passing it to the model.

Speed up your code like crazy!

Maxwell is a new kind of AI. It's a code execution model that speeds up your code on CPUs and GPUs.

"Code execution models" are a new category of AI. Maxwell is the first one, but this category will explode in popularity, and you'll see why.

Say you have a script that moves and processes some data.

You integrate your code with Maxwell, run it, and let it observe how it runs on your hardware and analyze the data your script moves around.

Maxwell will identify bottlenecks and look for faster algorithms and machine instructions for your workload. As long as your script runs, Maxwell rewrites the binary to make it faster.

In one example, Maxwell made a pandas pipeline 38.4x faster. It used more CPU cores, combined processing steps, reduced unnecessary memory reads and writes, and selected the right algorithms for the data the script was processing.

For example, imagine you want to check whether a number belongs to a collection. You could use hashing, but if the numbers occupy a small, dense range, a compact bitmap can make that check much faster.

In short, that's one of the algorithmic data-dependent tricks Maxwell can leverage to speed things up.

Here is the most impressive part of all of this:

Maxwell produces a machine-checked mathematical proof that each replacement preserves the original behavior.

Basically, any code they modify will always produce the same output as the old one.

This is really cool for anyone working on AI or data engineering workflows. You will squeeze much more work from the hardware without rewriting your application.

A Gemini-based agent found and formally verified new acceleration rules for eleven unresolved Turing machines in BB(6), the current frontier of the Busy Beaver problem.

Busy Beaver is uncomputable, so no fixed list of problems exists. The agent has to pick machines, spot patterns in their execution traces, and propose compact rules that summarize many steps at once.

fullText:
Which Minds Will Emerge Beneficial “Basic AI Drives” as they Become Superintelligent?
 
https://t.co/e8ug6mLTfa

(TL;DR -- the ones designed to have beneficial and self-stabilizing goal-systems from the get-go...)

In his 2008 "Basic AI Drives" paper, Steve Omohundro argued that almost any advanced AI will tend to improve itself, guard its goals, protect itself (including against being switched off) and grab resources, whatever goals it starts with, because those things help with nearly any goal. Much of today’s AI-risk thinking comes from this argument. 

My new blog post argues that it only holds for one kind of mind: a single-score maximizer that cares only about outcomes and has frozen, certain goals. It then runs Omohundro-style reasoning on a different sort of AI design -- one with many objectives, firm ethical limits, values woven deeply enough to grow back when damaged and held with some doubt, a gate that checks every change it makes to itself, and other minds around to check it. What comes out is nine beneficial drives, in many cases quite different in nature from Omohundro's selfish AI drives.

The key twist is that Omohundro’s own drives point the other way under my "BGI" assumptions. Goal preservation ends up defending good values. Doubt about its own judgment gives the system a reason to keep humans able to correct it, where Omohundro's assumptions imply an agent will near-inevitably get around such checks. And applying his reasoning to others’ goals, which it cares about but can’t fully know, gives a BGI agent a reason to protect, inform and empower the people around it, and to keep the world diverse.

None of this implies guaranteed BGI. Selfish and beneficial minds are both stable attractors, and a big enough shock can knock a system from one toward the other. Humans sit in an unstable middle btw selfish and beneficial, which is one reason to be wary of building superintelligent humanlike minds. The practical lesson is to build AGI designed from the start to meet the beneficial assumptions, keep on measuring the degree to which it actually does...

Here’s why agent swarms are going to be a very big deal. We can finally make compute a critical variable in a large number of important tasks in the economy which wasn’t possible before.

There’s a large amount of work in the world that is essentially only constrained by the amount of time that we put into research, data processing, discovery work, running tests, and more. All of this work is bottlenecked by our ability to plan, execute, review, and coordinate everything happening in these workflows. Which means we basically do very little of them today relative to their economic value. 

Agent swarms are the first real ability to parallelize this work in a way where - in theory - the only parameter that matters is how much compute you throw at the problem. Cyber security, life sciences or material science research, trading, QA testing, data processing, and many other fields are essentially compute constrained problems in the limit once models are good enough at these tasks.

The breakthrough is that in a world where agents can use tools, write code, process data, have strong domain depth, and can coordinate with each other, you can begin to solve arbitrarily complex problems by setting the right goals and applying enough tokens to the problem. This changes a lot of fields as well as even the competitive dynamics in these fields.

fullText:
Survivorship Bias — How a young statistician identified this cognitive bias and saved lives:

During World War II, the U.S. wanted to add reinforcement armor to specific areas of its planes.

Analysts examined returning bombers, plotted the bullet holes and damage on them (as in the image below), and came to the conclusion that adding armor to the tail, body, and wings would improve their odds of survival.

But a young statistician named Abraham Wald noted that this would be a tragic mistake.

By only plotting data on the planes that returned, they were systematically omitting the data on a critical, informative subset:

The planes that were damaged and unable to return.

• The "seen" planes had sustained damage that was survivable.
• The "unseen" planes had sustained damage that was not.

Wald concluded that armor should be added to the *unharmed* regions of the returning planes (the areas without bullet holes on the image below).

His profound logic: Where the survivors were unharmed was actually where the planes were most vulnerable.

Based on his insight, the military reinforced the engine and other vulnerable parts, significantly improving the safety of the crews during combat and saving thousands of lives.

Abraham Wald had identified a cognitive bias called "Survivorship Bias":

The error resulting from systematically focusing on survivors (successes) and ignoring casualties (failures) that causes us to miss the true base rates of survival (the actual probability of success) and arrive at flawed conclusions.

Survivorship Bias is all around us — its cost to business can be huge. 

What is unseen often has more value than what is seen.
